title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — Section 65 (Tampering with Computer Source Documents)

content.overview: Section 65 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 makes it an offence if any person knowingly or intentionally conceals, destroys or alters, or intentionally or knowingly causes another to conceal, destroy or alter, any computer source code used for a computer, computer programme, computer system or computer network, when the computer source code is required to be kept or maintained by law for the time being in force. Punishment is imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both, as the section provides.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Computer source code? (2) Required by law to be kept/maintained? (3) Knowingly or intentionally conceal/destroy/alter? (4) Punishment under s. 65?
content.study:
s. 65 is specific to source code required by law to be maintained. Ordinary code deletion without that legal keep requirement may fall under other provisions (e.g. s. 43/66) but not necessarily s. 65.

No new case invented.

sections.heading: Actus reus
sections.body: Conceal, destroy or alter computer source code, or cause another to do so.

sections.heading: Source code required by law
sections.body: The source code must be required to be kept or maintained by law for the time being in force.

sections.heading: Punishment
sections.body: Imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both — as enacted.

sections.heading: Method
sections.body: Identify source code; prove legal keep requirement; prove knowing/intentional act; apply punishment frame.

examples.title: Required source code destroyed
examples.body: Developer knowingly destroys source code that a sector regulation requires to be maintained — s. 65 ingredients may be made out.

hypotheticals.question: Does deleting any source code always attract s. 65?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. The source code must be required by law to be kept or maintained; otherwise other IT Act provisions may apply instead.

distinctions.title: s. 65 source code vs s. 66 computer-related offences
distinctions.left: Specific offence for tampering with source code required by law to be maintained.
distinctions.right: Criminalises dishonest/fraudulent commission of s. 43 acts generally.
